analysis.one_liner: Fines health insurers with high claim-denial rates and refunds the money to their customers.
analysis.headline: Introduced April 22, 2026, the bill was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the same day and has seen no action since, with one cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let the Health and Human Services Secretary fine health insurance companies that deny 25% or more of the claims in a plan year — $10 million plus $2 million for each percentage point above 25%. The fines would be split among that insurer's customers as refunds. Insurers would also have to tell customers, when they deny a claim as medically unnecessary, exactly what standards they used and why the claim failed, and report their denial rates to the government every year.
analysis.who_benefits: Customers of any insurer with high denial rates, who would get refunds when those denials are punished, plus any patient whose insurer must now explain a medical-necessity denial in writing.

how_it_helps.text: The Secretary can fine an issuer up to $10 million plus $2 million for every percentage point its claims denial percentage exceeds 25%, and every dollar collected must be distributed pro rata to the people enrolled in that coverage.

When an insurer denies a claim because the item or service was not medically necessary, it must send the patient a notice with its medical necessity standards and an explanation of why the claim failed.
Each insurer must report to the Secretary the percentage of claims denied under its coverage each plan year, and the Secretary may audit coverage to verify denial rates.
Claims denied for fraud or lack of medical necessity do not count against the insurer unless the insurer can show the Secretary enough evidence to prove the denial was correct.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers with denial rates at or above the threshold, who face penalties up to tens of millions of dollars and new reporting and notice duties — costs that could partly show up in premiums.

drawbacks.text: The penalty is capped at $10 million plus $2 million per percentage point over 25%, which is small relative to the revenues of large national insurers, so per-customer refunds could be modest even for heavily penalized plans.

The 25% trigger and the penalty amounts are left largely to the Secretary, who may set a lower threshold and may weigh an insurer's efforts to reduce denials, giving the industry room to argue for leniency in how the law is applied.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The refund mechanism is real but likely modest — the cap makes the fines a nudge rather than a devastating hit for the biggest insurers — while the transparency requirements, which force insurers to explain medical-necessity denials and publish denial rates, may be the more durable benefit for patients who currently get little or no explanation when a claim is refused.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote has been scheduled since.

narrative.text: Rep. Angie Craig introduced the bill on April 22, 2026, joined by one original cosponsor, Rep. Ryan, and the bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
The bill's only listed cosponsor is a Democrat, and no further action — no committee vote, hearing, or floor action — appears in the action history after the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill has not moved, health insurers with high denial rates remain free of any federal penalty tied to their denial rates, and the handful of members who backed the bill have so far gotten only a referral. If the bill never moves further, insurers benefit most from the delay.

for.name: Rep. Angie Craig
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to committee under her sponsorship; the lead author of the denial-rate penalty and refund scheme.

for.name: Rep. Ryan
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill as an original cosponsor at introduction.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the only cosponsor are Democrats, and no Republican support appears in the record; no vote has been taken, so the partisan shape of the House is unknown.

industries.note: Insurers would face civil fines for denial rates at or above 25% of claims, plus new duties to publish denial rates and explain medical-necessity denials in writing to patients. Insurers profit by collecting premiums and paying out less in claims, so a penalty keyed to the share of claims refused directly targets that revenue lever.

analysis.trajectory: The 119th Congress is still in session, but with one cosponsor and no committee action since the April 2026 referral, the bill's realistic path is to sit in the Energy and Commerce Committee until the Congress ends, unless its provisions get folded into a larger health package.
